solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Liberal workers sign without giving name (8)

indicators.note: 'without' means lacking: the sign has to go on without the letter N, the standard abbreviation for name

blocks.note: hands = workers, as in farm hands

annotation.surface: A Liberal Party's employees signing something anonymously.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Liberal' looks like the political party; here it is the adjective meaning generous.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain sense: liberal and handsome both describe a generous amount, as in a handsome or liberal reward.

clue.text: Hospital operation limiting unwell time? That’s a high point (7)

indicators.note: 'limiting' means forming the limit or boundary, so the operation sits at the far end of unwell and time

blocks.note: H = hospital, as on road signs

annotation.surface: A hospital operation that sets a limit on sick days, called a triumph.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A high point' suggests an achievement; it is literal, the top of a hill.
annotation.definitionFit: Literal reading: the summit of a hill is physically high, while the phrase usually means a best moment.

clue.text: Half-heartedly bribe an aristocrat (5)

indicators.note: 'heart' is the middle of a word, the double B here; 'half-heartedly' keeps only half of it

blocks.note: to nobble = to bribe or tamper with

annotation.surface: Someone half-heartedly trying to buy off a lord.
annotation.walkthrough: Nobble is British slang for bribing or tampering with a juror or racehorse. Its middle is the double B, and half of that goes.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: as a noun the word means a member of the titled class, a peer.

clue.text: Rocky rubble around shopping centres, note, as seen on TV? (5-6)

indicators.note: 'around' means encircling, so the rubble wraps round the shopping centres

blocks.note: scree = loose rocky debris on a slope

annotation.surface: A rocky landscape surrounding shopping malls, as featured in some television programme.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rocky' looks like the boxing film; here it just describes the rubble.
annotation.definitionFit: Metonym: television is nicknamed after the size of its display, against cinema's big screen.

clue.text: Illusory vision? I’m upset with anger (6)

indicators.note: 'upset' means knocked over, so in a down clue the letters are turned upside down, i.e. reversed
'with' means together with, so the anger word is attached after the reversed pair

annotation.surface: Someone angry and upset at seeing something that is not there.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Upset' reads as distressed; in a down clue it means turned upside down.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by description: desert heat bends light so a traveller sees water that is not there.

clue.text: Fool losing last friend (4)

indicators.note: 'losing last' means the word gives up its final letter, like a runner dropping off the end

blocks.note: CHUMP (a fool) without its last letter P

annotation.surface: Someone foolish losing their final friend.
annotation.walkthrough: A chump is a fool; cutting its tail leaves the friend.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: chum is informal British slang for a close companion.

clue.text: Teacher unacceptable? Leave (4,3)

blocks.note: the head = head teacher, the principal
that's a bit off = that's unacceptable

annotation.surface: A teacher's behaviour judged unacceptable, and told to leave.
annotation.walkthrough: In Britain the head is the school principal, and 'a bit off' means not acceptable.
annotation.definitionFit: Phrasal verb: this means setting out for somewhere, as in 'time to get going'.

clue.text: Satisfied about religious texts for choral setting (5)

indicators.note: 'about' means surrounding, so satisfied wraps round the religious texts

annotation.surface: Happy with the scriptures chosen for a piece of church music.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is all church music, and the answer usually sets religious words, so it belongs there.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: a short polyphonic choral piece, usually setting a sacred Latin text.

clue.text: Sign Liberal runs area (5)

blocks.note: Lib is the short form of Liberal

annotation.surface: A Liberal politician posts a notice for an area they run.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sign' reads as a verb, as if a Liberal were signing something; it is a star sign.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the scales are one of the twelve zodiac signs that horoscopes are written for.

clue.text: Damage after overturning some component of fortification (7)

indicators.note: 'overturning' means turning over, so the word for damage is read the other way round
'after' means following, so the second piece is placed behind the first in the answer

annotation.surface: Damage done after a piece of a fort was knocked over.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue sounds like a report of siege damage, so 'component of fortification' tempts as a single definition; only the last word defines.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the broad earth bank or wall round a castle is one kind of fortification.

clue.text: Different attempt to interrupt new version of some pantomime (6,5)

indicators.note: 'interrupt' means break into, so the two words are inserted into the middle of the other letters
a 'new version' is a rewritten one, so the letters of some are rearranged

annotation.surface: A fresh take on a pantomime, with some new attempt interrupting it.
annotation.walkthrough: A pantomime is a British Christmas stage show for families, full of fairy-tale characters.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: one of the stock British Christmas pantomimes, alongside Cinderella and Aladdin.

clue.text: Support odd instances of these (3)

indicators.note: 'odd' means odd-numbered, so only the letters in positions one, three and five are kept

blocks.note: keep letters 1, 3 and 5, dropping H and S

annotation.walkthrough: 'Support' is a golfing one: the peg under the ball before a drive.
annotation.definitionFit: A specific sense: the small peg on which a golfer rests the ball for the first shot holds it up.

clue.text: Escapes when it’s time for bed? (6,3)

blocks.note: to light out = to leave in a hurry
the dormitory or barracks call to switch off the lamps

annotation.surface: Children slipping away just when they are meant to go to bed.
annotation.walkthrough: The verb phrase is informal for running off, which lets it match 'Escapes'.
annotation.definitionFit: Two idioms: to light out is American slang for fleeing, and the call to switch off lamps marks bedtime.

clue.text: Friend with excellent luxurious residence (6)

annotation.surface: A friend who has a splendid, luxurious home.
annotation.walkthrough: A straightforward pair of synonyms joined end to end.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by description: a monarch's or bishop's grand official home is the model of luxury living.

clue.text: The French island: certain to offer relaxation (7)

annotation.surface: A French island promoted as a sure place to unwind.
annotation.walkthrough: Reads like a holiday advert, which suits the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: free time spent at ease, rather than at work, is relaxation.

clue.text: Live link initially with small creatures in location of bats? (6)

indicators.note: 'initially' means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word is taken

annotation.surface: Living alongside little creatures in a place where bats roost.
annotation.walkthrough: The 'small creatures' look like the bats themselves; fry are baby fish.
annotation.definitionFit: Idiom: 'bats in the belfry' means crazy, because bats roost in church bell towers.

clue.text: Back half of cemetery we rebuilt, incorporating English cemetery plant? (3,4)

indicators.note: 'back half' means the rear half, so the last four of the eight letters are kept
'rebuilt' means put together again differently, so these letters are rearranged
'incorporating' means taking into its body, so the E is absorbed inside the rearranged letters

blocks.note: the last four of CEMETERY's eight letters

annotation.surface: The rear of a graveyard being rebuilt around an English tree.
annotation.walkthrough: The setter uses 'cemetery' twice on purpose: once as letters, once in the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: yews are the trees traditionally grown in English churchyards, hence the question mark.

clue.text: It may appear when sportsman needs a rest (6)

definitions.text: It may appear when sportsman needs a rest

blocks.note: the surface pictures an athlete in general; the setter means a snooker player
the surface reads as needing a break; in snooker a rest is a stick that supports the cue, and one kind stands on tall legs to arch over balls

annotation.surface: An athlete taking a break, and something turning up.
annotation.walkthrough: The 'rest' seems to be a break; in snooker it is a cue support, and the answer is the kind that arches over balls.
annotation.definitionFit: Specialist sense: snooker players use several cue rests, and this one has tall legs to bridge over balls.

clue.text: African country doctor taken aback about one test subject (6,3)

indicators.note: 'aback' means backwards, so the doctor's letters are taken in reverse
'about' means surrounding, so the reversed doctor wraps round the letter for one

blocks.note: GP = general practitioner, a family doctor

annotation.surface: A country doctor in Africa startled by an experiment.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Country doctor' looks like one phrase; 'African country' is the unit, and the doctor is a GP. 'Taken aback' means surprised on the surface.
annotation.definitionFit: Idiom: the rodent was once the standard laboratory animal, so any person tried out on is called by its name.

clue.text: Enthusiasm filling us today? Not entirely (5)

indicators.note: 'not entirely' means only in part, so the answer is part of the letter string, not the whole

annotation.surface: Wondering whether we feel much enthusiasm today.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Filling' looks like the container instruction; it is part of the letter string, and 'Not entirely' is the signal.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: from the Italian for taste, it means keen relish or enthusiasm.

clue.text: Bitter conflict recalled (3)

indicators.note: 'recalled' read as re-called means called back, so the word is spelt backwards

annotation.surface: Memories of a bitter conflict.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bitter conflict recalled' reads as a war remembered; the last word is the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A weather sense: a raw wind or day is damp and biting, just as a bitter one is.

clue.text: Proportion scoundrel presented with binary digits (5)

blocks.note: 1 and 0, read as the letters I and O

annotation.surface: A share of the loot for a rogue handed some computer code.
annotation.walkthrough: Binary uses only the digits 1 and 0, which look like I and O.
annotation.definitionFit: Mathematical sense: it expresses how one quantity stands to another, like 3 to 1.

clue.text: Got a tan around end of August? Very surprised (7)

indicators.note: 'around' means encircling, so the word for got a tan wraps round the single letter
'end of' means the final part, so only the last letter of the month is used

annotation.surface: Someone astonished at their late-summer suntan.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface puts August in a holiday picture; only its last letter is used.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym with intensity: this is surprise strong enough to leave you briefly unable to react.

clue.text: Animal Patronus at first abandoning boy wizard (5)

indicators.note: 'at first' means at the beginning, so only the opening letter of Patronus counts
'abandoning' means leaving, so that letter departs from the wizard's surname

annotation.surface: A Harry Potter-world animal guardian deserting the boy wizard.
annotation.walkthrough: A Patronus is a spirit-animal charm in Harry Potter, and Hermione's takes this very form, so the answer fits the scene.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: this river mammal is one example of an animal, and the Potter setting makes it an apt one.

clue.text: Debut for Oxford United due (4)

indicators.note: a 'debut' is a first appearance, so it gives the first letter of the next word

annotation.surface: A player's first game for Oxford United football club is coming up.
annotation.walkthrough: Oxford United is an English football club; the clue splits it, taking O from Oxford and reading United as married.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a payment that is still outstanding has fallen due, and both words work as adjectives.

clue.text: Regrets blocking activity by the writer producing horror (8)

indicators.note: 'blocking' means obstructing from inside, so regrets sits in the middle of the activity word
'by' means beside, so the writer's pronoun is simply placed alongside

blocks.note: go = activity, as in 'always on the go'

annotation.surface: Remorse stopping a writer's work that turns out to be a horror story.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The writer' is the crossword convention for the setter, so ME.
annotation.definitionFit: Descriptive sense: something grisly enough to provoke horror in whoever sees it.
